keyIdeas: Strategy is the skill of making higher-level decisions while anticipating competitor moves.
Sequential games are solved by backward induction: look forward and reason backward.
Simultaneous games are solved by looking for dominant strategies and Nash equilibrium.
Cheap talk should not be trusted when interests are completely misaligned.
Repeated interactions can make reputation matter.
Asymmetric information includes adverse selection, screening, signaling, and moral hazard.
Moral hazard is addressed by making the informed actor bear some consequences.
Good segments are identifiable, reachable, stable over time, and profitable.
Mass market strategy fits homogeneous needs.
Adjacent segment strategy targets the most similar segment first.
Niche strategy is useful when large dominant players ignore a segment.
Breaking an industry norm can be useful when the dominant segmentation approach no longer fits.
In horizontal differentiation, greater differentiation can support higher equilibrium profits.
In one-period Bertrand competition with homogeneous products, zero marginal cost, and no capacity limits, both firms price at marginal cost and earn zero profit.
Finite repeated interaction does not sustain collusion theoretically; infinite repetition can sustain it through trigger strategies if firms are patient enough.
Collusion is harder when deviation gains are high, detection is weak, punishment is small, or punishment lacks credibility.
Loyalty programs and targeted rebates can soften price competition.
Strategic cooperation can involve complements, most-favored-customer clauses, deep price cuts, loyalty programs, and targeted rebates.
Unobservable sales effort is a moral hazard problem.
A bonus can induce high effort when the expected incremental bonus covers the cost of effort.
In alternating-offer bargaining, patience is summarized by the discount factor delta = 1 / (1 + r).
When counteroffers can be made very quickly, bargaining shares approach an even split.
The bargaining pie is the extra surplus above the parties' outside options.
Bargaining can fail because parties misperceive outside options or the cost of waiting.
The golden rule of pricing is (price - marginal cost) / price = 1 / elasticity.
Higher price elasticity implies a lower optimal price.
Price discrimination requires limited resale, imperfect information, or high transaction cost.
First-degree price discrimination charges each consumer their maximum willingness to pay.
Third-degree price discrimination uses observed characteristics and charges lower prices to high-elasticity groups.
Second-degree price discrimination uses menus and self-selection, requiring individual rationality and incentive compatibility.
English, Japanese, and Vickrey auctions can produce the same revenue under standard assumptions; Vickrey bidding strategy is to bid value.
High quality can be signaled by actions low-quality firms find too costly to copy.
Quality signals include money-back guarantees, extended warranties, high prices, advertising, and reputable retailers.
Interlacing product lines reduces differentiation, while segmentation keeps differentiation high.
Product launch timing trades off first-mover advantage against premature launch risk.
Umbrella branding lowers cost and lends image to the new product, but failure can damage the brand.
Use umbrella branding when new-product quality is coherent with brand image; create a new brand when quality is too dissimilar or risk is high.
The golden rule of advertising links advertising-to-revenue ratio to profit margin and demand elasticity with respect to advertising.
Advertise more when markup is high or demand is very sensitive to advertising.
Retailers control final price, in-store advertising, service, returns, and customer access.
Vertical integration can reduce double marginalization and lower consumer prices compared with separate manufacturer-retailer markups.
Retailers provide services, geographic coverage, infrastructure, customer access, and competency.
Two-part tariffs with wholesale price equal to marginal cost can solve double marginalization while transferring surplus through a fixed fee.
With retail competition, prices may be too low and service too high from the manufacturer's perspective.
